title: The science of men
hookLine: scholars wrote lives of the narrators, to test each one

cards: A story is told about the hadith scholar Ali ibn al-Madini. Someone asked him about a narrator, and the narrator was his own father. He hesitated, and said: ask someone else.
They pressed him. And he answered, as the story goes: this is the religion. My father is weak.

Whatever the details, the story shows what a whole field of study asked of people: a son choosing accuracy over family pride. Behind that answer stood a library of judgments about people. Today, the science of men.

teach.h: RIJAL: THE PEOPLE IN THE CHAINS.
teach.b: Rijal means men, and in hadith study it names the narrators themselves, the people in the chains. Despite the word, the books include women who narrated too.
Why it began: in the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the early scholar Ibn Sirin is quoted saying, in effect, people didn't use to ask about chains.

Then came the time of turmoil, and they said: name your men for us. And again: this knowledge is religion, so look at whom you take your religion from. What the books record: entry after entry, narrator by narrator.
Where he lived. Whom he heard from, and who heard from him. Whether he traveled.
Was he truthful? Was his memory precise, or did it slip, or fade late in life? Did he write his reports down, and keep the pages safe?
The field has a blunt name: al-jarh wa al-ta'dil, wounding and vouching. Each narrator could be wounded by a scholar's criticism, or vouched for. Then a hard question, faced openly.

Isn't talking about a man's flaws a kind of backbiting? Imam Muslim answers in that same introduction: exposing a narrator's weakness, to protect what's said in the Prophet's name, isn't forbidden backbiting. It's a duty.
Out of this came books of narrators that students of hadith still open. When a scholar grades a report, this is the shelf behind the grade.

how: Hadith scholars consult biographical dictionaries of narrators, the books of rijal, to check each name in a chain for honesty, memory and whom they met, a field called al-jarh wa al-ta'dil.

games.q: you're a hadith scholar, and someone asks you about a narrator. he's your own father, and his memory is weak. what do you say?
games.why: as the story of Ali ibn al-Madini goes, he hesitated, then said: this is the religion. my father is weak.

practice: Pick one voice you trust for information, a news outlet, a teacher, a channel, a friend who always knows things, and quietly ask the rijal questions: where do they get what they tell me, have they been wrong and said so, do details drift, do they have a reason to shade the story?
You're not putting them on trial, only writing a short entry in your own book of narrators. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in judging.
